title: Identification of Genes and Haplotype Analysis in Soybean Using Next-Generation Sequencing
author: Zhu, Tian
materials: Online platform for querying haplotype analysis

Timing: 1 h
3.Install all required software in a Linux environment, preferably using Conda. We applied multiple complementary population genetic metrics to ensure robust detection of selective signals:a.Weir and Cockerham’s FST, calculated using VCFtools, to measure pairwise population differentiation.b.π ratio, computed with VCFtools, to identify regions exhibiting reduced nucleotide diversity indicative of selective sweeps.c.XP-CLR (Cross-Population Composite Likelihood Ratio) analysis, performed using the XP-CLR software, to detect cross-population selection based on allele frequency differentiation.d.RAiSD (Raised Accuracy in Sweep Detection), used to capture signatures of selective sweeps by modeling local distortions in the site frequency spectrum and linkage disequilibrium. # environment.yml name: python_env channels: - bioconda - conda-forge - defaults dependencies: - python=3.7 - bwa=0.7.18 - trimmomatic=0.39 - samtools=1.20 - gatk4=4.2 - vcftools=0.1.16 - xpclr - beagle=5.4 # Utilities - wget - unzip # Note: RAiSD is NOT available through conda. # mkdir RAiSD && cd RAiSD # wget https://github.com/alachins/raisd/archive/master.zip # unzip master.zip # cd raisd-master # chmod +x install-RAiSD.sh # ./install-RAiSD.sh CRITICAL: Ensure that the following software versions are compatible to prevent conflicts during analysis. When version mismatches occur or dependencies cannot be resolved, install individual tools in separate Conda environments.

steps.title: Obtain raw resequencing data
steps.instruction: Collect soybean whole‑genome DNA sequencing FASTQ files (published or newly generated) and verify that each sample has accompanying metadata (accession ID, geographic origin, population, experimental design). Ensure the sequencing depth is at least 5× and that library preparation, platform, and read length documentation are provided.

steps.title: Verify data integrity and quality
steps.instruction: For each FASTQ file: (a) check completeness with the provided MD5 checksum; (b) confirm filenames match the metadata sheet; (c) run FastQC on a subset to inspect base quality distribution, adapter contamination, and read length. Exclude or request replacement for any sample that fails these checks before proceeding.

steps.title: Install software environment (≈1 h)
steps.instruction:
Create a Conda environment (e.g., python_env) on Linux and install the exact versions listed: python=3.7, bwa=0.7.18, trimmomatic=0.39, samtools=1.20, gatk4=4.2, vcftools=0.1.16, xpclr, beagle=5.4, wget, unzip. RAiSD is not in Conda; download and install it manually:
```
mkdir RAiSD && cd RAiSD
wget https://github.com/alachins/raisd/archive/master.zip
unzip master.zip
cd raisd-master
chmod +x install-RAiSD.sh
./install-RAiSD.sh
```
Verify that all tool versions are compatible; if conflicts arise, use separate Conda environments for conflicting tools.

steps.title: Compute windowed nucleotide diversity (π) (≈3 h)
steps.instruction:
Prepare inputs: (a) filtered biallelic VCF named `input.filtered.vcf` (MAF/missingness filtered); (b) two population ID lists `popA.list` and `popB.list` (one ID per line); (c) gene annotation `reference.gff`; (d) utility scripts `zscore.py` and `GetGeneFromGFF.py`. Create a shell script `run_pi.sh` that runs VCFtools windowed‑π for each population with 100 kb windows and 100 kb steps:
```
ls *.list | while read plist; do
  echo "nohup vcftools \
    --vcf input.filtered.vcf \
    --keep ${plist} \
    --window-pi 100000 \
    --window-pi-step 100000 \
    --out ${plist%.list} &"
 done > run_pi.sh && sh run_pi.sh
```

steps.title: Identify common windows and compute π‑ratio
steps.instruction:
Extract window keys for each population and intersect them:
```
grep -v BIN popA.windowed.pi | awk '{print $1"_"$2"_"$3}' | sort > A.keys
grep -v BIN popB.windowed.pi | awk '{print $1"_"$2"_"$3}' | sort > B.keys
comm -12 A.keys B.keys > common.keys
```
Tag each π table with its composite key:
```
awk '{print $1"_"$2"_"$3, $0}' popA.windowed.pi > A.tag
awk '{print $1"_"$2"_"$3, $0}' popB.windowed.pi > B.tag
```
Pull rows for the common windows:
```
while read k; do grep -w "$k" A.tag; done < common.keys > A.common
while read k; do grep -w "$k" B.tag; done < common.keys > B.common
```
Join the tables and calculate the π‑ratio (π_A / π_B):
```
paste A.common B.common | awk '{print $2, $3, $4, $6, $12, $6/$12}' > popA_vs_popB.piratio
```
Sort and keep only the final columns:
```
grep -v BIN popA_vs_popB.piratio | sort -k1,1n -k2,2n | awk '{print $1, $2, $3, $6}' > popA_vs_popB.piratio.in
```

steps.title: Standardize π‑ratio and select outliers
steps.instruction:
Run Z‑score standardization on the π‑ratio file:
```
python zscore.py popA_vs_popB.piratio.in popA_vs_popB.piratio.in.zscore
```
Extract windows with significant Z‑scores (Z ≥ 1.96):
```
awk '$5 >= 1.96 {print $1, $2, $3}' popA_vs_popB.piratio.in.zscore > popA_vs_popB.piratio.in.zscore.pos
```
If chromosome names differ from the GFF, normalize them (e.g., add leading zeros):
```
awk '{printf("Chr%02d %s %s\n", $1, $2, $3)}' popA_vs_popB.piratio.in.zscore.pos > popA_vs_popB.piratio.in.zscore.pos.norm
```

steps.title: Map outlier windows to genes and clean list
steps.instruction:
Map the normalized outlier intervals to genes using the provided script:
```
python GetGeneFromGFF.py reference.gff popA_vs_popB.piratio.in.zscore.pos.norm popA_vs_popB.piratio.in.zscore.pos.genes
```
Extract unique gene IDs and remove attribute strings:
```
awk '{print $9}' popA_vs_popB.piratio.in.zscore.pos.genes | grep -v attr |
  sed 's/ID=//g' | sed 's/;//g' | sort -u > popA_vs_popB.piratio.in.zscore.pos.genes.clean
```

steps.title: Integrate candidate genes across methods (≈5 min)
steps.instruction:
Collect all gene‑list files (each with one clean gene ID per line, no header) into the working directory. Set the support threshold K (e.g., K=2):
```
K=2
```
Merge and count support:
```
cat *.outlier.genes.clean | sort | uniq -c > gene.counts.tmp
```
Genes supported by at least K methods:
```
awk -v k=$K '{if ($1 >= k) print $2}' gene.counts.tmp > consensus.k${K}.genes
```
(Optional) genes supported by exactly K methods:
```
awk -v k=$K '{if ($1 == k) print $2}' gene.counts.tmp > consensus.eqk${K}.genes
```

steps.title: Extract target interval from per‑chromosome VCFs
steps.instruction:
For the interval of interest (e.g., Chr2:50394718-50402312) pull records from every per‑chromosome VCF (bgzipped, tabix‑indexed) and sort:
```
ls ../vcf/soybean.*.Chr*.vcf.gz | while read v; do
  tabix "$v" Chr2:50394718-50402312
done | sort -k2,2n > interval.records
```
Capture a VCF header once:
```
zcat ../vcf/soybean.X.Chr2.vcf.gz | grep '^#' > header.vcf
```
Assemble a minimal interval VCF:
```
cat header.vcf interval.records > interval.raw.vcf
```

steps.title: Phase/impute interval VCF with Beagle
steps.instruction:
Run Beagle (v5.4) on the assembled interval VCF to obtain a phased VCF (output compressed):
```
beagle gt=interval.raw.vcf out=interval_beagle
# produces interval_beagle.vcf.gz
```

steps.title: Call haplotypes per sample
steps.instruction:
Execute the provided Python script `haplo.py` on the phased VCF to generate a haplotype table:
```
python haplo.py interval_beagle.vcf.gz > interval.haplo
```
The script loads all biallelic sites with complete genotypes, builds a per‑sample haplotype string, and prints each unique haplotype (Haplotype1, Haplotype2, …) together with the list of member samples.

steps.title: Count haplotypes by region/population (≈5 min)
steps.instruction:
For each region list (e.g., `regionA.list`) count how many samples belong to each haplotype (here up to Haplotype5 as an example):
```
for k in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  cat regionA.list | while read sid; do
    grep -w "$sid" interval.haplo
  done | grep -w "Haplo${k}" | wc -l
done
```
Repeat the loop for each region list (regionB.list, etc.). Ensure sample IDs match exactly (case‑sensitive) between the VCF and the region list files.

description: This protocol leverages publicly available soybean resequencing data collected from multiple studies deposited in NCBI and the National Genomics Data Center of China. To ensure reliable detection of selected genes and accurate haplotype analysis, raw sequencing data must meet strict quality standards (e.g., high-quality genome resequencing data with sufficient sequencing depth, uniform coverage, and minimal missing sites to ensure completeness and accuracy). Detailed sample information, including accession identifiers, geographic origin, and population metadata, should be verified and curated prior to downstream analysis.
